question: Assume today is 2026-08-19. You know nothing published after this date. Estimate the number of registered company insolvencies in England and Wales in August 2026 (the headline monthly total of compulsory liquidations, creditors' voluntary liquidations, administrations, company voluntary arrangements and receivership appointments, in which the first three are seasonally adjusted), as it will be first reported in the Insolvency Service's monthly Company Insolvency Statistics release.

target.what: Headline monthly total of registered company insolvencies in England and Wales reported in the Insolvency Service's monthly Company Insolvency Statistics release for August 2026: sum of compulsory liquidations, creditors' voluntary liquidations (CVLs), administrations, company voluntary arrangements
target.caveats: Target period is future relative to the 2026-08-19 cutoff, so no August 2026 data exist yet; the estimate must be built from pre-cutoff history, seasonality, and leading signals. assessment.note: All are SA headline monthly totals for England and Wales from the same Insolvency Service series. They form the primary level anchor: 2025 ran ~2,000-2,230, early 2026 dipped (Jan 1,764, Feb 1,907, Mar 2,037, Apr 2,085), then May/Jun 2026 fell to 1,849/1,845. p72 (June 2025 = 2,048) is the same series as p20 but a different vintage; both agree at ~2,050, so no conflict.

Component breakdowns of the headline for Aug 2025 and Jun 2026. They sum to the headline (Aug 2025: 311+1,600+121+16+0 = 2,048; Jun 2026: 276+1,364+191+14 = 1,845). Confirms the headline is a sum of these channels and that CVLs dominate (~74%).

Month-on-month and year-on-year changes for June 2026 components. p82 (administrations +45% m/m) is explained by p83 (~60 connected real-estate companies), so the June administration spike is a one-off, not a trend signal. CVLs and compulsory liquidations both down ~15% y/y, consistent with the lower 2026 headline.

12-month rolling insolvency rates per 10,000 companies. They drift gently (52.5 -> 51.8 -> 50.5 by June 2026), confirming a mild downward trend in the rate, not a collapse. p84 (50.5, year to June 2026) is the most recent and consistent with the lower 2026 monthly totals.

HR1 redundancy-notice forms by month. August 2025 (p62 = 285) is a clear seasonal trough vs spring/autumn (~400+), corroborating an August seasonal dip in insolvency activity. HR1 is a leading/administrative trace, not the target itself.

HMRC winding-up petitions up 31% y/y and ~2,400 court-ordered liquidations in the past year suggest upward pressure on compulsory liquidations, which conflicts with the observed ~15% y/y fall in compulsory liquidations (p80) and the lower 2026 headline. Possible explanations: petition-to-order lag, or petitions settled before order. Treated as an upside risk to compulsory liquidations only, not a level anchor.

Distress indicators (zombie firms, critical financial distress, sector distress in hotels/bars) and 2025 totals. They point to elevated but not accelerating distress; p55 (23,938 in 2025, broadly in line with 2024) supports a flat-to-slightly-down level into 2026. These are qualitative/contextual, not direct monthly inputs.
Both cite the 2008-09 peak rate of 113.1 per 10,000; identical figure from the same source, so they are one fact, not two. Useful only as a distant upper bound; current rate (~50) is far below it.

methods.label: m1
methods.rationale: August 2025 (p1) scaled by the April 2026/April 2025 ratio (p41/p43). April is the latest month with a same-month prior-year comparator in the kept set, so it carries the most recent y/y growth signal (~+2.8%). This route assumes the y/y growth measured in April 2026 transfers to August 2026; it does not use the May-June 2026 decline, so it likely sits at the high end. Shared dependency: all input

methods.label: m2

p41.role: April 2026 SA headline total, England and Wales, company insolvencies

a2.role: change factor from April 2026 to August 2026

methods.rationale: Anchors on the most recent spring level (April 2026, p41 = 2,085) and applies a change factor reflecting the observed May-June step-down (~1,847) plus August seasonal softness. Failure mode: if the May-June dip was a one-off reporting effect, this under-predicts. Shared dependency with m1 on the same SA series.

methods.label: m3

p1.role: August 2025 SA headline total, England and Wales, company insolvencies

a1.role: change factor from August 2025 to August 2026

methods.rationale: Same-month seasonal analogue: August 2025 (p1 = 2,048) times a y/y change factor. The factor is informed by the ~10% y/y fall in May-June 2026 (p70 vs p72) and the falling rolling rate (p84), tempered by HMRC petition upside (p86). This is the most direct seasonal route because it inherits August's own seasonal position. Failure mode: a structural break in the 2026 y/y trend between June and Augus

weight_basis.m1: B1 of 3 blocks; median of blocks: not the median (one vote, counts in the interval)
weight_basis.m2: B2 of 3 blocks; median of blocks: this block is the median
weight_basis.m3: B3 of 3 blocks; median of blocks: not the median (one vote, counts in the interval)

combination.weight_gate: off: inverse backtest-error weights need a bank-level gate (>= 30 scored questions with >= 2 backtested routes, hit rate >= 0.7; METHODS_ZH 4.1), which has not been run

interval.rule: several blocks: root mean square of the block widths, times the Birge ratio when it exceeds 1

baseline.rule: seasonal naive: the target's value for the same calendar period last year

kept.name: August 2026 level relative to August 2025
kept.rationale: 2026 monthly totals (May 1,849, Jun 1,845) are ~10% below the same months of 2025 (p70 vs p72), and the rolling rate fell from 52.5 to 50.5 (p32 vs p84). August 2025 was 2,048 (p1). A modest further decline or stabilisation is the central case; HMRC petition growth (p86) is an upside risk, hence the
kept.applies_when: The 2026 y/y decline observed in May-June persists into August without a sharp enforcement-driven rebound.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence that compulsory liquidations surge in mid-2026 (e.g. HMRC petition orders converting at a high rate) or that CVLs re-accelerate to 2025 levels.

kept.name: August 2026 level relative to April 2026
kept.rationale: April 2026 was 2,085 (p41); May and June fell to ~1,847 (p70, p71), a ~11% drop. August typically sits below spring (HR1 August trough, p62). Central case assumes the post-April step-down is largely retained with a small seasonal August dip.
kept.applies_when: The May-June 2026 step-down is a level shift rather than a one-off, and August shows its usual seasonal softness.
kept.falsified_by: A July 2026 rebound back toward 2,000+ or evidence that the May-June dip was a reporting artefact.

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
